title: Why ice floats
prompt:
Explain to a seven-year-old why ice floats on water, even though ice is made of water.

Write exactly 3 sentences. Write 25 to 60 words.

Words are counted by the spaces between them. A sentence ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.

answer.authorNote: Three sentences leave room for one cause and its effect. A strong answer says what is odd about freezing (the water spreads into a roomier pattern), what follows from that (more room, same stuff, so lighter for its size), and then gives an everyday picture to hold on to.
answer.example: When water freezes, its tiny pieces lock into a roomy, open pattern with empty gaps in between. Those gaps make a block of ice take up more room than the same water did. Bigger and lighter for its size, the ice has to sit on top, like a beach ball in a bath.

hints: What changes about the tiny pieces of water when it freezes?
If the same water takes up more room, what happens to how heavy it feels for its size?
What everyday object floats because it is light for its size?
solution:
One example answer (53 words):

> When water freezes, its tiny pieces lock into a roomy, open pattern with empty gaps in between. Those gaps make a block of ice take up more room than the same water did. Bigger and lighter for its size, the ice has to sit on top, like a beach ball in a bath.

Each sentence does one job: what freezing does, why that matters, and a picture to remember. The beach ball makes the idea something a child can hold.
